subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Counting Coconut Trees and Cups in Arrays

tasks_in_class.description: Count the coconut trees in Gundappa's land from the top-view grid. Write the number. How do you know?
Count the number of cups Muniamma has made and write the number.
How many coconut laddoos are there in the trays?
Gundappa plucked 5 coconuts from each tree. How many coconuts has he plucked?

time_bands.activity: Children look at the top-view grid of coconut trees in the book. Each child quietly counts and writes the number, then shares with a neighbour how they counted — row-by-row, column-by-column, or some other grouping. The teacher asks two or three children to explain their method aloud: Let Us Count, p.34 ("Count the coconut trees… How do you know?")

The class turns to Muniamma's stacked cups. Children count and record, then move to the laddoo trays. For each picture the teacher asks: 'Did you count one-by-one or in groups? Which was quicker?' Small groups compare answers. Let Us Count, p.34 ("Count the number of cups…") and Let Us Count, p.34 ("How many coconut laddoos are there…?")

Children use small counters or finger-groups to re-enact the laddoo tray: they lay counters in equal rows and skip-count to verify. The teacher circulates and presses: 'How does arranging in rows help you count faster?' Let Us Count, p.34 ("How many coconut laddoos are there in the trays?")

The multiplication problem is posed: if Gundappa plucks 5 coconuts from each tree, how many has he plucked? Children write their working and share strategies. Two or three methods are displayed on the board and compared. Let Us Count, p.34 ("Gundappa plucked 5 coconuts from each tree. How many coconuts has he plucked?")

periods.teacher_notes: The core idea this unit builds is that arranging objects in equal rows or groups makes counting faster and reveals multiplicative structure. Watch for children who count every object one-by-one even after grouping is available — prompt them with 'Can you skip-count the rows?' Note: T-5 (milk pedas) is an additional counting task identical in structure to T-4; it can be set as extra practice for early finishers.
materials: Counters or small objects (20–30 per pair)

periods.activity_title: Counting and Arranging Play Money in Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Look at Shirley's coin arrangement (circular pattern). How much money is it?
Look at Shiv's notes-and-coins grid arrangement. How much money is it?
How did you count them? Discuss in class.
Arrange play money of amounts 1, 2, 5, and 10 to show ₹36, ₹125, and ₹183. Ask your peers to tell how much it is.
Shirley and Shiv arranged coins in groups. Write the number of coins in the blank triangles for each arrangement.

time_bands.activity: Children open the book to p.35 and study Shirley's circular coin arrangement and Shiv's grid arrangement. Each child writes the total for each arrangement. The teacher asks: 'Did you count each coin separately, or did you group them?' Patterns with Money, p.35 ("Look at Shirley's coin arrangement… How much money is it?") and ("Look at Shiv's notes-and-coins grid arrangement. How much money is it?")

A class discussion: children share how they counted. The teacher records two or three different strategies on the board (e.g., counting by denomination, adding rows). The class compares which is quickest and why arrangement helps. Patterns with Money, p.35 ("How did you count them? Discuss in class.")

Pairs use play-money sets (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 coins and notes) to build ₹36, then ₹125, then ₹183 on their desks. The partner looks at the arrangement and names the total without touching it. Pairs swap roles. Patterns with Money, p.35 ("Arrange play money… Ask your peers to tell how much it is.")

Children fill in the blank triangles in the Two Ways arrangement diagram, writing the number of coins in each group for Shirley's and Shiv's arrangements. The teacher asks: 'The total is the same — why do the groups look different?' Two Ways, p.35 ("Write the number of coins in the blank triangles for each arrangement.")

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight this unit develops is that the same quantity can be arranged in different grouping patterns, and the arrangement reveals how counting proceeds. A common error is children adding the denomination values rather than the number of coins; clarify whether the task asks for number of coins or total value in each case.
materials: Play-money sets (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 denominations — one set per pair)

periods.activity_title: Pairing Coins to Discover Even and Odd

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36
tasks_in_class.description: Describe Shiv's arrangement and write his numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36
tasks_in_class.description: Describe Shirley's arrangement and write her numbers.
Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.
Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?

time_bands.activity: Each child takes a small handful of counters and pairs them up. The teacher models: 'Shiv's coins all pair perfectly — nothing is left. Shirley's coins always have one left over.' Children look at p.36 and describe each arrangement in their own words, then write Shiv's numbers. Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36 ("Describe Shiv's arrangement and write his numbers.")

Children describe Shirley's arrangement: coins that cannot all be paired leave one remaining. They write her numbers. The teacher connects the vocabulary: numbers that pair perfectly are called even; those with one left over are called odd. Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36 ("Describe Shirley's arrangement and write her numbers.")

Children work through numbers 1–20, drawing pairing lines or using counters to decide even or odd, and record in two lists. Early finishers skip-count in 2s and notice what they land on. Even and Odd, p.36 ("Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.")

The class recites the 2-times table together, then children circle each product and check whether it is in the even list. The teacher opens the inquiry: 'Is every number in the 2-times table even? How can we be sure?' Children discuss in pairs and share. Even and Odd, p.36 ("Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?")

periods.teacher_notes: The pairing model is the conceptual anchor for even and odd — children should use physical counters before moving to the drawn or listed form. A frequent error is calling 0 odd; if it arises, pair 0 counters together and show nothing is left over. The times-2 inquiry plants the generalisation developed more formally in the next section.
materials: Squared paper or blank paper for drawing pairs

periods.activity_title: From Pairing to the Crayons Chart: Classifying Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set (5, 8, 36, 69, 22, 51, 30, 38, 37, 52, 43). Use the crayons arrangement if needed.
Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen. Draw a square on the even page numbers. Put a circle on the odd page numbers.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the crayons chart (1–50) from p.37: odd numbers in one column, even in the adjacent column. Children scan the chart and describe what they see — 'all the numbers ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 are on one side.' The visual structure is discussed before any writing begins. Crayons Arrangement, p.37 ("Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number…")

Children classify the given set of numbers (5, 8, 36, 69, 22, 51, 30, 38, 37, 52, 43) by circling odd and squaring even, referring to the chart when uncertain. Pairs compare and reconcile any difference. The teacher asks: 'Without the chart, how would you decide?' Crayons Arrangement, p.37 ("Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set…")

Children flip through several pages of their textbook and mark page numbers — square for even, circle for odd. They share Shirley's observation: left-hand pages are always even, right-hand pages are always odd (or the reverse). The teacher asks: 'Why does this happen? What does it tell us about consecutive numbers?' Crayons Arrangement, p.37 ("Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen…")

periods.teacher_notes: Children who built the even-odd lists through pairing in the previous topic now apply that understanding to classify larger numbers using the chart's visual structure. A common error is classifying by the tens digit rather than the units digit; prompt children to look only at the last digit of the number when using the chart.
materials: Pencils or coloured pencils for circling and squaring

periods.activity_title: Neighbours of Even and Odd: Investigating Consecutive Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders if numbers before and after an even number are odd. Check and discuss.
Choose any 10 consecutive numbers. Write whether they are even or odd below each number. What do you notice? Discuss.

time_bands.activity: Children pick three odd numbers of their choice, write the number before and after each, and label all three as even or odd. They repeat for three even numbers. The teacher collects results on the board. The class reads Shirley's and Shiv's claims and checks them against the board data. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders…")

Each child chooses a starting number and writes 10 consecutive numbers. Below each they write E or O. Pairs compare their strips: 'Do yours look the same? What pattern do you see?' The teacher brings a few strips to the board and the class reads the alternating pattern together. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Choose any 10 consecutive numbers. Write whether they are even or odd…")

The class tries to state the pattern as a rule in their own words: 'Even and odd numbers take turns.' The teacher then poses a what-if: 'If I tell you 47 is odd, what can you say about 48 and 46 without checking?' Children respond and justify. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Choose any 10 consecutive numbers… What do you notice? Discuss.")

periods.teacher_notes: The investigation of neighbours anchors the alternating pattern that the crayons chart made visible. Children sometimes think the neighbour rule applies only to small numbers; press them to try starting numbers above 50 or 90 to build confidence in generalising. Encourage children to articulate the rule in their own words before the teacher states it.
materials: Strips of paper or notebooks for writing consecutive number sequences
Board space for collecting class results

periods.activity_title: Units-Digit Rule and Making Even Numbers from Digits

tasks_in_class.description: Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99.
Make two 2-digit numbers using digits 1 and 6 without repetition; identify as even or odd. Then choose any two digits and make 2-digit even numbers.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 300 on the board and asks: 'Is this even or odd? How do you know without the crayons chart?' Children discuss and identify that the units digit (0) determines the answer. They work through 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99, writing a reason for each. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning…")

Children form 16 and 61 from digits 1 and 6, classify each, and explain why using the units digit. They then choose their own two digits, form as many 2-digit numbers as possible, and circle those that are even. The teacher asks: 'Which digit must be at the units place for the number to be even?' Even and Odd, p.38 ("Make two 2-digit numbers using digits 1 and 6 without repetition… make 2-digit even numbers.")

Pairs share their digit-combination findings. The class pools examples and the teacher guides articulation: 'A number is even if its units digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.' Children verify this against two or three of the numbers from the first task. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Make two 2-digit numbers using digits 1 and 6 without repetition…")

periods.teacher_notes: The units-digit rule is the chapter's most generalisable takeaway — children move from the pairing model to a digit-based shortcut for classifying any whole number. A common error is checking the tens digit rather than the units digit for large numbers like 300 or 415; use the pairing vocabulary ('what would the units digit look like if you tried to pair them?') to reconnect.
materials: Digit cards (0–9, two sets per pair)

periods.activity_title: Counting Even and Odd Numbers from 1 to 100

tasks_in_class.description: Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the question as a genuine puzzle: 'Between 1 and 100, are there more even or more odd numbers?' Children make a quick guess and record it. Groups of four share their guess and the reasoning behind it before any counting begins. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?")

Each group decides on a strategy — listing, skip-counting, using the crayons chart, or using the alternating-pattern rule. They count and record. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How confident are you? Can you check a different way?' Groups using different methods are noted for the discussion to follow. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?")

Groups share results and methods. The class reconciles: from 1 to 100 there are exactly 50 even (2, 4, …, 100) and 50 odd (1, 3, …, 99) numbers. The teacher draws out the argument from the alternating pattern: every pair of consecutive numbers contributes one even and one odd, so the counts are equal. Children write the conclusion in their own words. Even and Odd, p.38 ("Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?")

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings the alternating-pattern insight to a satisfying quantitative conclusion. The key move is helping children see that the argument from the alternating pattern is more powerful than exhaustive listing. Watch for groups that count 1–99 instead of 1–100; the inclusion of 100 (even) keeps the totals balanced and is worth addressing explicitly.
materials: Crayons chart (p.37 of textbook, or a class-made chart on paper)
Notebooks for recording strategies and counts

periods.activity_title: Chapter Consolidation: Patterns, Money, and Even-Odd Reasoning

tasks_in_class.description: How many milk pedas are there in the trays?
Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.
Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99.

time_bands.activity: Children count the milk pedas in the tray picture and compare strategies: did they count row-by-row, column-by-column, or by equal groups? The teacher connects this opening to the chapter's theme — arrangement reveals pattern. Let Us Count, p.34 ("How many milk pedas are there in the trays?")

Children revisit the pairing model and list numbers 1–20 as even or odd, drawing pairs where helpful. The teacher then holds a quick oral round: teacher calls a number, children say even or odd and give the units digit as reason. Even and Odd, p.36 ("Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.")

Children classify 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99 using the units-digit rule and write a reason for each. Pairs check each other's work. The class discusses any disagreements. The teacher closes by asking: 'Which single idea from this chapter helps you decide if any number is even or odd?' Even and Odd, p.38 ("Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning…")

periods.teacher_notes: This consolidation unit draws on the chapter's progression from grouping objects to the digit-based classification rule, giving children who need more practice a further opportunity and those who are secure a chance to articulate their reasoning clearly. The most common residual confusion is classifying large numbers by a digit other than the units digit; the oral round in the middle band surfaces this quickly.
materials: Textbooks (for the peda-tray picture and pairing tasks)
Notebooks or mini-whiteboards for oral round responses

items.prompt: Mango trees are planted in 4 rows with 6 trees in each row. Draw the arrangement in your notebook. Count the trees by grouping in rows and write the total.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There are 24 mango trees. Counting 6 trees in each of the 4 rows: 6, 12, 18, 24.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group objects into equal rows and skip-count to find the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them use counters to build the array; stretch: ask them to draw a different arrangement that gives the same total.

exercise.description: Count the coconut trees in Gundappa's land from the top-view grid. Write the number. How do you know?

items.prompt: Cups are stacked in 5 columns with 3 cups in each column. How many cups are there? Write how you counted.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There are 15 cups. Counting 3 in each column for 5 columns: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Skip-count equal groups (columns) to find the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the columns and circle each group of 3; stretch: ask what happens if one more column of 3 is added.

exercise.description: How many coconut laddoos are there in the trays?

items.prompt: Priya arranges her coins: three ₹5 coins and four ₹2 coins. Which of the following shows the total amount?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each denomination by its count, then add the two groups.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added the number of coins (3 + 4 = 7) to one denomination (₹5 × 3 = ₹15) incorrectly, or confused counts with values.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied the total number of coins (7) by ₹4 — merging the two denominations into one.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted only the ₹2 coins correctly (₹8) but used only ₹1 × 6 for the ₹5 coins, suggesting a denomination confusion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them lay out play-money coins and physically count each group; stretch: ask them to make ₹23 a different way using the same denominations.

exercise.description: Arrange play money of amounts 1, 2, 5, and 10 to show ₹36, ₹125, and ₹183. Ask your peers to tell how much it is.

items.prompt: Open any page in your textbook. Write the page number. Is it even or odd? How do you know by looking at which side of the book the page is on?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Right-hand pages have odd numbers and left-hand pages have even numbers (or the reverse, depending on book). The student should identify the pattern correctly for their book and use the page position as evidence.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the page-position pattern (left or right side of book) to classify the page number as even or odd.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to check three pages in a row and list the numbers; stretch: ask them to predict whether page 47 will be on the left or right side without opening to it.

exercise.description: Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen. Draw a square on the even page numbers. Put a circle on the odd page numbers.

items.prompt: Asha counts ₹2 coins by making groups of 4. Ravi counts the same coins by making groups of 2. They get the same total. Explain why both methods give the same answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both methods give the same total because the number of coins and the value of each coin do not change — only the grouping changes. Grouping differently is a different way of counting the same amount.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The total value depends on the number and denomination of coins, not on how they are grouped for counting.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to act it out with play coins in two different groups and count each time; stretch: ask what would happen if Asha made groups of 3 — would she still get the same total?

exercise.description: How did you count them? Discuss in class.

items.prompt: Shiv arranges 12 coins in groups of 4. Shirley arranges the same 12 coins in groups of 3 and groups of 5. How many coins are in each of Shirley's groups? Write the number in each group for her arrangement.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shirley has one group of 5 and one group of 3, then repeats: for 12 coins one possible split is two groups of 5 (= 10) and one group of 2 — or the student may list two groups of 3 and two groups of 3 summing to 12. Accept any grouping using 3s and 5s that sums to 12, e.g. one group of 5 + one group of 5 + one group of 2 is not valid (no group of 2 allowed); valid: one group of 3 + three groups of 3 = 12, or two groups of 3 + one group of 6 — the key constraint is groups of 3 and 5 only. Simplest correct answer: two groups of 3 and two groups of 3 (all groups of 3, summing to 12), or one group of 5 + one group of 5 + one group of 2 — but since only 3 and 5 are stated, the correct answer is: two groups of 3 and — this cannot sum to 12 using only 3s and 5s without remainder. Correcting: 3+3+3+3 = 12 (four groups of 3). Accept four groups of 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add groups of the given sizes repeatedly until the total matches the number of coins.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give them 12 counters to physically arrange; stretch: ask them to find a different grouping using only 3s and 5s that also totals 12.

exercise.description: Shirley and Shiv arranged coins in groups. Write the number of coins in the blank triangles for each arrangement.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Every number in the 2-times table is even.' Which of the following best explains why this is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Because 2 is an even number, so all its multiples end in 2.

options.label: B
options.text: Because even numbers are the ones we say when skip-counting by 5.

options.label: C
options.text: Because multiplying any number by 2 gives a number that can be arranged in pairs with nothing left over.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the 2-times table only has numbers smaller than 20.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. Multiplying any number by 2 means making 2 equal groups, so the total can always be arranged in pairs with nothing left over — that is the definition of an even number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the pairing model: a multiple of 2 is always a number that forms complete pairs.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student over-generalises from 2's units digit; multiples of 2 end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, not only 2.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student mistakes the scope of the 2-times table, confusing a finite list for all multiples.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates even numbers with skip-counting by 5, mixing up two different skip-counting patterns.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to pair up counters for 6, 8, and 10 and confirm nothing is left over; stretch: ask whether 2 × 13 is even and how they know without pairing.

exercise.description: Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?

items.prompt: Meena picks the number 35. She says: 'The number before 35 and the number after 35 are both even.' Is she correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because 34 is odd and 36 is even, so only one neighbour is even.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because odd numbers cannot have even neighbours.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because 35 ends in 5, so its neighbours end in 4 and 6, which are even.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, but only for numbers that end in 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A. 34 ends in 4 (even) and 36 ends in 6 (even), so both neighbours of 35 are even. This holds for every odd number, not only those ending in 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the units digit of each neighbour to classify it as even or odd.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not yet accepted the alternating pattern and thinks odd numbers cluster together.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student overfits the rule to units digit 5, not realising the neighbour pattern holds for all odd numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has mis-classified 34 as odd, likely checking the tens digit (3) rather than the units digit (4).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to write 34, 35, 36 and underline the units digit of each; stretch: ask them to find an odd number whose neighbours are NOT both even, and explain why they cannot.

exercise.description: Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders if numbers before and after an even number are odd. Check and discuss.

items.prompt: Which of the following numbers is even? Choose the correct answer and explain using the units digit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300. Its units digit is 0, which is even. All the other numbers have odd units digits (5, 7, 9).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Look at the units digit only; if it is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 the number is even.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be looking at the hundreds digit (4) rather than the units digit (5).
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be looking at the tens digit (6) rather than the units digit (7).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may recognise 9 as odd but has not applied the rule consistently, possibly guessing.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: underline the units digit of each number together before deciding; stretch: ask them to write the smallest and largest 3-digit even number whose hundreds digit is 5.

exercise.description: Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99.

items.prompt: From 1 to 10, write all the even numbers and all the odd numbers. Are there more even or more odd numbers? What do you notice about the count?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Even numbers from 1 to 10: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — five numbers. Odd numbers from 1 to 10: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 — five numbers. There are equal numbers of each. The alternating pattern means every pair of consecutive numbers contributes one even and one odd.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List even and odd numbers separately, then count each list to compare.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to write 1–10 in a row and alternate shading even and odd; stretch: ask whether the same result holds for 1 to 20 or 1 to 50, and how they know without listing all of them.

exercise.description: Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?

items.prompt: Which of the following numbers is odd?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9. When 9 counters are arranged in pairs, one is always left over. Its units digit is 9, which is odd.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pair counters or check the units digit to determine if a number is odd.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have confused 14 with a number that leaves a remainder when paired, possibly miscounting.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may not yet have linked multiples of 10 to the even category.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be guessing or has not connected units digit 6 to even.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw 9 dots and pair them to see the leftover; stretch: ask them to write the next odd number after 9 and explain how they found it.

exercise.description: Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.

items.prompt: Look at the numbers below. Which group contains only even numbers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8, 22, 36, 52. All four numbers have a units digit of 8, 2, 6, or 2 respectively — all even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the units digit of every number in the group; all must be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student missed that 51 ends in 1 (odd), possibly reading the tens digit instead.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student missed that 5 ends in 5 (odd), perhaps grouping it with even numbers because it is small.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student missed that 69 ends in 9 (odd), perhaps reading only the tens digit 6.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to underline the units digit of each number before deciding; stretch: ask them to create their own group of four even numbers where no two have the same units digit.

exercise.description: Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set (5, 8, 36, 69, 22, 51, 30, 38, 37, 52, 43). Use the crayons arrangement if needed.

items.prompt: Baskets of bananas are arranged in 3 rows with 7 baskets in each row. Each basket holds 4 bananas. How many bananas are there in all?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: First find the total number of baskets by counting equal rows, then multiply by the number of bananas in each basket.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: solve in two steps using a number line or repeated addition (7 + 7 + 7 = 21, then 21 groups of 4); stretch: change the number of rows to 5 and re-solve, then compare the two answers.

exercise.description: Gundappa plucked 5 coconuts from each tree. How many coconuts has he plucked?
